Content:
Suppose we have a discrete random variable [MATH: X] with probability mass function [MATH: f_X] and support [MATH: S_X = \{-1,0,1\},] shown below.

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: f_X(x)] | [MATH: 0.25] | [MATH: 0.5] | [MATH: 0.25] |

Content:
Now suppose that we define a new random variable [MATH: Y] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: Y = (X+1)^3.]

Content:
Computing [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y]] is quite a lot of work if we use only the methods we've seen up to now. Typically, we would need to find the probability mass function [MATH: f_Y] of [MATH: Y,] and then compute [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y].]

Content:
Thankfully, there is a handy rule, called the rule of the lazy statistician, that allows us to compute [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y]] without having to find [MATH: f_Y] first! This is useful because [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y]] might be the only quantity we're interested in.

Content:
The rule of the lazy statistician states that if [MATH: Y = r(X),] then

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[Y] = \sum_{x \in S_X}r(x) \, f_X(x).]

Content:
Applying the rule of the lazy statistician with the function [MATH: r(x) = (x+1)^3] for our PMF [MATH: f_X,] we have

Content:
[MATH: E[Y]|= ∑_(x ∈ S_{X})r(x)f_{X}(x); = ∑_(x ∈ S_{X})(x + 1)^{3}f_{X}(x); = (− 1 + 1)^{3} ⋅ 0.25 + (0 + 1)^{3} ⋅ 0.5 + (1 + 1)^{3} ⋅ 0.25; = 0^{3} ⋅ 0.25 + 1^{3} ⋅ 0.5 + 2^{3} ⋅ 0.25; = 0 ⋅ 0.25 + 1 ⋅ 0.5 + 8 ⋅ 0.25; = 0 + 0.5 + 2; = 2.5]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y] = 2.5.]

[MATH: \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \sum_{x \in S} r(x) f(x).]

[MATH: f(x) = 2x, \qquad 0 < x < 1.]

[MATH: f(x) = 2x, \qquad 0 < x < 1.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For a continuous random variable [MATH: X] and a function [MATH: r(x),] the rule of the lazy statistician states that

[MATH: \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \int^{\infty}_{-\infty} r(x)f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.]

In our case, we have

[MATH: r(X)=x^2-3x+3.]

Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: E[X^{2} − 3X + 3]|= ∫_{− ∞}^{∞}r(x)f(x)dx; = ∫_{0}^{1}(x^{2} − 3x + 3) ⋅ 2xdx; = ∫_{0}^{1}(2x^{3} − 6x^{2} + 6x)dx; = [(x^{4})/(2) − 2x^{3} + 3x^{2}]_{0}^{1}; = [(1)/(2) − 2 + 3] − 0; = (3)/(2).]

items.title: Applications of LOTUS

sections.normalized_html: A stick of length [MATH: 1] is broken at a point chosen uniformly at random along its length. Calculate the expected length of the shortest piece.
sections.readable_text: A stick of length [MATH: 1] is broken at a point chosen uniformly at random along its length. Calculate the expected length of the shortest piece.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For a continuous random variable [MATH: X] and a function [MATH: r(x)], the rule of the lazy statistician states that

[MATH: \textrm{E}[r(x)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} r(x)f(x) ~ \textrm{d}x,]

where [MATH: f(x)] is the probability density function of [MATH: X.]

In this problem, the break point [MATH: X] is chosen uniformly from [MATH: [0,1]], so the probability density function is

[MATH: f(x) = 1, \:\:\:\:\:\: 0 \leq x < 1.]

When the stick is broken at point [MATH: X], it is divided into two pieces: one of length [MATH: X] and the other of length [MATH: 1-X.] The shorter of the two pieces, [MATH: Y], is therefore given by

[MATH: Y = \textrm{min}(X, 1-X).]

Therefore, we define

[MATH: r(x) = \textrm{min}(x,1-x).]

To evaluate the integral, we express [MATH: r(x)] as an explicit piecewise function. Observe that,

  • if [MATH: 0\leq x < \dfrac{1}{2}], then [MATH: x < 1-x], so the shorter piece has length [MATH: x],

  • if [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2} \leq x \leq 1], then [MATH: x \geq 1 - x], so the shorter piece has length [MATH: 1-x.]

Therefore,

[MATH: {x,|0 ≤ x < (1)/(2),; 1 − x,|(1)/(2) ≤ x ≤ 1.]

We now apply the rule of the lazy statistician:

[MATH: E[Y]|= E[min(X, 1 − X)]; = ∫_{− ∞}^{∞}r(x)f(x)dx; = ∫_{0}^{(1)/(2)}x ⋅ 1dx + ∫_{(1)/(2)}^{1}(1 − x) ⋅ 1dx; = ∫_{0}^{(1)/(2)}xdx + ∫_{(1)/(2)}^{1}(1 − x)dx; = [(x^{2})/(2)]_{0}^{(1)/(2)} + [x − (x^{2})/(2)]_{(1)/(2)}^{1}; = (1)/(2)((1)/(2))^{2} + [(1 − (1)/(2)) − ((1)/(2) − (1)/(2)((1)/(2))^{2})]; = (1)/(8) + [(1)/(2) − ((1)/(2) − (1)/(8))]; = (1)/(8) + (1)/(8); = (1)/(4).]

Therefore, the expected length of the shorter piece is [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{4}}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we have a discrete random variable [MATH: X] with probability mass function [MATH: f_X] and support [MATH: S_X = \{-1,0,1\},] shown below.

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: f_X(x)] | [MATH: 0.25] | [MATH: 0.5] | [MATH: 0.25] |

Content:
Now suppose that we define a new random variable [MATH: Y] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: Y = (X+1)^3.]

Content:
Computing [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y]] is quite a lot of work if we use only the methods we've seen up to now. Typically, we would need to find the probability mass function [MATH: f_Y] of [MATH: Y,] and then compute [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y].]

Content:
Thankfully, there is a handy rule, called the rule of the lazy statistician, that allows us to compute [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y]] without having to find [MATH: f_Y] first! This is useful because [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y]] might be the only quantity we're interested in.

Content:
The rule of the lazy statistician states that if [MATH: Y = r(X),] then

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[Y] = \sum_{x \in S_X}r(x) \, f_X(x).]

Content:
Applying the rule of the lazy statistician with the function [MATH: r(x) = (x+1)^3] for our PMF [MATH: f_X,] we have

Content:
[MATH: E[Y]|= ∑_(x ∈ S_{X})r(x)f_{X}(x); = ∑_(x ∈ S_{X})(x + 1)^{3}f_{X}(x); = (− 1 + 1)^{3} ⋅ 0.25 + (0 + 1)^{3} ⋅ 0.5 + (1 + 1)^{3} ⋅ 0.25; = 0^{3} ⋅ 0.25 + 1^{3} ⋅ 0.5 + 2^{3} ⋅ 0.25; = 0 ⋅ 0.25 + 1 ⋅ 0.5 + 8 ⋅ 0.25; = 0 + 0.5 + 2; = 2.5]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: \textrm{E}[Y] = 2.5.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Some Comments

Content:
The rule of the lazy statistician states that if [MATH: Y = r(X),] then

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[Y] = \sum_{x \in S_X}r(x) \, f_X(x).]

Content:
Note the following points:

Content:
- The reason for the name "the rule of the lazy statistician" is that the rule is sometimes mistaken as a definition when, in fact, it is a statement that requires rigorous proof (we won't do that here).
- The rule is sometimes called the law of the unconscious statistician (or LOTUS).
- In general [MATH: \textrm E[r(X)] \ne r(\textrm E[X]).]

Content:
The rule has some nice intuition behind it. We demonstrate with a simple example.

Content:
Suppose a spinner has four sides, labeled [MATH: 1] through [MATH: 4.] Let the random variable [MATH: X] equal the result when the spinner is spun once, and let the function [MATH: Y = r(X)] denote the profit made when the spinner lands on [MATH: X = x.] To calculate the expected profit on each spin, we multiply each possible payout by the probability of that payout occurring and sum over all possible values of [MATH: X.]

Content:
Let's take a look at another example.

---

Item 3 — Example: Applying the Rule of the Lazy Statistician for Discrete Random Variables

Example Prompt:
A discrete random variable [MATH: X] has the probability mass function [MATH: f(x)] shown in the table below. Find [MATH: \textrm{E}\big[5e^{1-X}\big].]

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: 0.2] | [MATH: 0.8] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For a discrete random variable [MATH: X] and a function [MATH: r(x),] the rule of the lazy statistician states that

[MATH: \textrm{E}[r(X)] = \sum_{x \in S} r(x) f(x).]

In our case, we have

[MATH: r(x)=5e^{1-x}.]

Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: E[5e^{1 − x}]|= ∑_(x ∈ S)5e^{1 − x} ⋅ f(x); = 5e^{1 − 1} ⋅ 0.2 + 5e^{1 − 2} ⋅ 0.8; = 5e^{0} ⋅ 0.2 + 5e^{− 1} ⋅ 0.8; = 5 ⋅ 0.2 + 5e^{− 1} ⋅ 0.8; = 1 + 4e^{− 1}; = 1 + (4)/(e).]

Item 7 — Example: Applying the Rule of the Lazy Statistician for Continuous Random Variables

EXPLANATION
